newsitem.title: DENMARK: More than a million gas-powered vehicles on roads.
newsitem.headline: More than a million gas-powered vehicles on roads.

text.p: COPENHAGEN, June 12, Reuter - The number of vehicles powered by natural gas worldwide passed the one million mark last year, the World Gas Conference heard this week, but penetration of the car market remains tiny at just 0.1 percent of the total.

A report for a committee charged by the International Gas Union to look at gas as a transport fuel and chaired by Anzaour Skhaliakho of Russia's State Oil and Gas Academy said that practically every car manufacturer has now developed one or more types of Natural Gas Vehicle (NGV). But only a few are offering NGVs for sale commercially.

The advantage of gas as a transport fuel is that it is cleaner burning than gasoline or diesel, producing fewer emissions. The conference was also told that because gas is transported by underground pipelines to filling stations, it avoids the need for road tankers, contributing both to safety and to the environment.
But the development of the NGV fleet worldwide remains patchy. Argentina is the greatest user, with nearly 400,000 vehicles using 504 filling stations. The fleet is less than 10 years old there.

"In 1990 the NGV fleet was numbered in the hundreds. The present monthly increase in vehicle numbers is about 4000," the report said, adding that the programme there was based on converting cars from conventional fuels rather than making new vehicles.
The market is driven by a wide fuel cost differential between gas and oil products based on environmental concern.

Italy is also a large centre for NGVs, with 300,000 converted vehicles on the road after a programme first started 50 years ago. Annual fuel sales there account for 310 million cubic metres, approximately 0.5 percent of all vehicle fuel sales by value. Although only 1 percent of vehicles across the country run on natural gas, in some areas it is as high as 10 percent.

Russia is also taking a lead in NGV use, with 200,000 vehicles on the road using 187 filling stations. All of these have been built since 1987, the report said, and by 1990 Russia was using 511 million cubic metres of gas as a transport fuel.

A programme is underway to increase the number of refuelling stations to 1,000 by 2005, and to 2,500 by 2015. By 2000, Russia planes to convert 5,000 city buses in Moscow and elsewhere to run on Compressed Natural Gas (CNG).

In Russia as in Argentina, the tax structure is used to make CNG attractive as a vehicle fuel. The price is fixed at 50 percent of the price of gasoline by government decree, and there is also a state programme in place to develop the use of gas for tractors, diesel locomotives, river boats, and even for planes and helicopters.
Elsewhere the picture is less rosy, with Argentina, Italy and Russia between them accounting for some 90 percent of all NGVs worldwide.

The report concludes that increased use of natural gas would be desirable not just because of its environmental benefits but also as a means of reducing dependency on oil products to which there are no really well established alternatives. But the take up rate in most of the world remains slow.
